annotations.keyFindings: Booked or documented meetings showed no difference in 30-day readmission (17.8 against 18.4 percent), but meetings attended by family with a written plan were followed by 13.1 percent readmission.
annotations.limitations: Matching on age, ward and month only; complexity drove selection; the attended subgroup was defined after the fact.

annotations.keyFindings: In a worked example the crude odds ratio of 1.35 for enhanced discharge planning became 0.82 after adjustment for prior admissions, frailty and living alone.
annotations.limitations: One worked example; a methods commentary rather than an evaluation.

annotations.keyFindings: In five trials, structured family involvement reduced 30-day readmission (pooled risk ratio 0.84); unadjusted observational studies tended to show the opposite.
annotations.limitations: Interventions ranged from a phone call to a structured meeting; search ended in 2022.

annotations.keyFindings: Sampling two controls per case cut note reading by about 80 percent with the odds ratio changing by less than 5 percent; two readers agreed well on family attendance (kappa 0.81).
annotations.limitations: One hospital and one exposure; readers aware of readmission status coded borderline notes differently.

annotations.keyFindings: Counts of family conferences in three hospitals and staff views; no outcome after discharge.
annotations.limitations: No selection criteria, no outcomes, no dates, staff views only.
annotations.notes: Not rated: the summary reports no methods, outcomes or dates, so neither relevance to readmission nor method quality can be judged.

annotations.keyFindings: Carers valued meetings booked with notice and ending with a written plan; working carers and carers without transport often could not attend.
annotations.limitations: Two hospitals; carers recruited through ward staff.

annotations.keyFindings: In 140 patients, readmission within 30 days was 12 percent with a meeting and 21 percent without (p equal to 0.09).
annotations.limitations: Selection, age range, comparability and adjustment not reported; no year.
annotations.notes: Not rated: the abstract does not report the population, how patients were selected or any adjustment, so relevance and quality cannot be judged.

claims.text: In two hospitals, readmission within 30 days was 13.1 percent after meetings that the family attended and that produced a written plan, against 18.4 percent in matched patients without a meeting.
claims.passage: When the analysis was restricted to meetings that a family member attended and that produced a written plan, readmission was 13.1 percent against 18.4 percent.
claims.interpretation: The exposure worth measuring is an attended meeting with a written plan, not a booked meeting.

claims.text: Adjusting for prior admissions, frailty and living alone reversed a crude harmful-looking association of enhanced discharge planning with readmission.
claims.passage: the crude odds ratio of 1.35 became 0.82 after adjustment for prior admissions, frailty and living alone
claims.interpretation: Complexity must be measured and adjusted for, or the meetings will look harmful.

claims.text: Sampling two controls per readmitted case cut note reading by about 80 percent with little change in the estimate, and family attendance could be read reliably from notes.
claims.passage: Sampling controls at a ratio of two per case reduced note reading by about 80 percent compared with reviewing every discharge, and the odds ratio for the exposure changed by less than 5 percent.
claims.interpretation: Case-control sampling fits the 120 hours available for reading notes.

claims.text: In randomised trials, structured family involvement in discharge planning reduced 30-day readmission.
claims.passage: In the trials, structured family involvement reduced 30-day readmission (pooled risk ratio 0.84, 95 percent CI 0.71 to 0.99).
claims.interpretation: A modest benefit is plausible; the trial interventions were more structured than local practice.

claims.text: Working carers and carers without transport often could not attend daytime discharge meetings.
claims.passage: Many working carers could not attend weekday daytime meetings, and carers without a car found the hospital hard to reach
claims.interpretation: Attendance partly reflects carers' circumstances, which matters for both confounding and equity.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, five appraised at abstract level and two left unrated. Trials show a modest reduction in readmission with structured family involvement, while observational comparisons of booked meetings show no difference, probably because meetings are chosen for complex patients; adjustment for complexity reversed a harmful-looking crude estimate in a worked example. Meetings attended by the family and ending with a written plan were followed by lower readmission in one matched comparison. Note reading can identify attendance reliably, and sampling two controls per case keeps reading affordable. Two undated grey records report no usable methods and are not rated.
gradeRationale: Trials support a modest benefit of structured family involvement, but local-type evidence on meetings is observational with serious confounding by complexity, and two records could not be rated. Certainty that an attended meeting with a written plan reduces readmission is low.
summary: Seven retrieved records; five appraised, two undated records left unrated with no scores; five claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.
